label: Response inhibition
summary: The capacity to withhold a prepared response — indexed by No-Go accuracy. Consistently weaker at higher ADHD-trait load, even below clinical thresholds.

label: Statistical learning
summary: Implicit extraction of environmental regularities — the habit-learning system. Indexed by faster responses to high-probability triplets.

label: Inhibition–learning antagonism (competition hypothesis)
summary: The trade-off in which weaker inhibitory control normally buys stronger statistical learning. The paper's central object of study.

label: ADHD as a trait continuum
summary: The dimensional view: ADHD-like traits are distributed across the general population, and neurocognitive shifts appear before symptoms reach clinical significance. The frame that makes a screening score meaningful without a diagnosis.

label: Cue as motivational magnet (sign-tracking)
summary: Borrowed from animal sign-tracker/goal-tracker work: at high trait load the cue itself captures behaviour and top-down systems cannot override it — the authors' proposed reason the learning advantage breaks down.

label: Mind-wandering
summary: Spontaneous shift of attention from external demands to internally generated thought; offered as a second, transdiagnostic candidate mechanism.

label: Anxiety-driven arousal
summary: Chronic anxious arousal produces internal churn that is phenomenologically near-identical to internal hyperactivity, and frequently co-occurs with ADHD. The single most important thing to rule out here.

label: Sleep debt / disrupted sleep
summary: Insufficient or fragmented sleep degrades attention and produces restlessness — a mimic that must be excluded before attributing symptoms to ADHD.

label: Mood disturbance (depression / chronic stress)
summary: Depression and chronic stress produce concentration difficulty and inner agitation. Another mimic on the differential.

label: Sustained attention / vigilance
summary: The capacity to maintain attention on a task over time. A mechanism-level axis, indexed by continuous performance tests; lapses show up as reaction-time variability.

label: Working memory
summary: Holding and manipulating information over short intervals. One of the dissociable neurocognitive routes to ADHD-like presentation; indexed by n-back and complex-span tasks.

label: Reward processing / delay aversion
summary: The motivational pathway: an aversion to waiting and steeper discounting of delayed rewards. Partly independent of the inhibitory route; indexed by delay-discounting paradigms.

label: Arousal / state regulation
summary: Regulation of physiological and cognitive arousal. The axis ADHD shares most with its mimics — anxiety, sleep debt and mood all perturb it, which is why they overlap ADHD at the phenotype. The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep and noise, so the overlap is by construction; the putatively ADHD-specific part is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

label: Excessive spontaneous mind-wandering
summary: Constant, topic-unstable internal mental activity, proposed to arise from altered default-mode deactivation and DMN–executive interaction. Measured by the MEWS; targets the form rather than the content of thought. Its ADHD-specificity is contested — it also tracks anxiety.

label: Reaction-time variability
summary: Intra-individual variability in response speed — a robust and heavily replicated ADHD marker, but not specific to ADHD relative to other clinical groups.

label: Temporal processing / timing
summary: Perception and reproduction of time intervals. A third dissociable component in multiple-pathway models, independent of inhibition and delay aversion.

label: Cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly sluggish cognitive tempo)
summary: A construct of attention decoupling from the external context — staring, daydreaming, mental fogginess, slowed thinking and hypoactivity. Distinct from ADHD inattention in factor-analytic work and more strongly tied to internalizing (depression) than to hyperactivity/impulsivity, which makes it a rival reading of a foggy, disengaged 'internal state' rather than an anxious, churning one.

label: Emotional dysregulation
summary: Difficulty modulating emotional responses — lability, low frustration tolerance, quick temper, slow return to baseline. Prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major driver of impairment, proposed to arise from deficits in attention to emotional stimuli. It overlaps anxiety and mood by construction, so it both deepens the ADHD phenotype and blurs the boundary with the mimics; whether it is core to ADHD or a distinct dimension is unsettled.

label: Default-mode network interference
summary: A neurobiological model in which spontaneous low-frequency default-mode-network activity, normally suppressed during tasks, intrudes into task-positive processing and produces periodic attentional lapses. Proposed as a substrate for reaction-time variability and inattention, it links the mind-wandering and vigilance axes to a specific network rather than a single region.

label: Delayed circadian phase
summary: A shift of the internal clock later than the day's demands — delayed dim-light melatonin onset, delayed sleep period, chronic sleep-onset insomnia. Distinct from acute sleep debt: it is a rhythm problem, not just a quantity problem. Highly prevalent in ADHD and proposed by some as intrinsic to a subgroup rather than merely comorbid, which is what makes it more than a mimic.

label: Reproductive-hormone modulation of ADHD symptoms
summary: Fluctuations in estradiol, progesterone and testosterone across the menstrual cycle (and, by extension, puberty, pregnancy and menopause) modulate ADHD symptom expression in women — lower estradiol tracks worse symptoms. A source of within-person variability specific to females, absent from male-referenced models, and a reason symptom severity can move without the underlying trait changing.

label: Executive function
summary: The set of self-regulatory control processes — response inhibition, working memory, sustained attention, planning and self-monitoring — that organise goal-directed behaviour. In leading theory ADHD is a primary executive/inhibition deficit, but empirically EF weakness is neither universal in ADHD nor specific to it, and lab EF tests capture it poorly relative to real-world ratings.

label: Rejection sensitivity
summary: A cognitive-affective disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive, and overreact to social rejection or criticism. A validated general-psychology construct (not ADHD-specific), studied across depression, anxiety and personality disorders; in ADHD it is treated as a facet of emotional dysregulation. Distinct from the popular label 'rejection sensitive dysphoria', which names the same experience but lacks the construct's evidence base.

label: Hyperfocus / difficulty disengaging attention
summary: Intense, long-lasting absorption in a task with reduced awareness of surroundings and time, and difficulty shifting attention away from it. Reframes ADHD attention as dysregulated allocation — attention over-deployed as well as under-deployed — rather than a simple deficit. Elevated in ADHD but not specific to it (also invoked for autism and schizophrenia), and still inconsistently defined and measured.

label: Reward-motivation / reinforcement sensitivity
summary: How reward and incentive drive behaviour — proposed to be altered in ADHD, with reduced dopamine reward-pathway function and an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement. Manifests as strongly contingency-dependent performance (reward, interest and urgency lift it) rather than a fixed capacity deficit. Related to but broader than delay aversion, which concerns the timing of reward specifically.

label: Atypical sensory processing (hyper-/hyposensitivity)
summary: Over- or under-responsiveness to sensory input — sound, light, texture, touch — and difficulty modulating it. Elevated in ADHD in both directions (hyper and hypo), dimensionally related to ADHD trait level, and present irrespective of autistic symptoms, though it is also a core feature of autism and thus not specific. A plausible contributor to distractibility and to sensory-driven restlessness.
